_about: Lucky Monkey rules. Edit, then `tools/deploy.sh data` (seconds, no rebuild). Missing keys fall back to the built-in copy. See docs/ for what each part means.

workers.name: Mango
workers.role: Field technician: good at everything. Runs any response at normal speed.

workers.name: Pip
workers.role: Scout: flies straight over the void and diagnoses twice as fast; too small for heavy work.

workers.name: Moss
workers.role: Maintenance: twice as fast at preventive work (certificates, patches, clean-ups, canaries).

workers.name: Fern
workers.role: Hardware: twice as fast with cables, vents and power; hops quickly between nodes.

workers.name: Tusk
workers.role: Heavy lifter: deploys, rollbacks, databases and replicas twice as fast; never forgets a runbook.

tutorial.coach: A service crashed. Press Space (or click the 💻 terminal) and pick 🔄 Restart: a crew member runs it. Left alone, it starts hurting its neighbours.
Names don't resolve but IPs work: that's DNS. Not sure? 🍌 H buys a hint, or 🔍 I diagnoses.
A WARNING: nothing is broken yet. Renew the certificate before the timer hits; Moss 🦥 is fastest at maintenance.
Two at once! Each crew member runs one thing at a time, so both can be handled in parallel.
Two at once! Each crew member runs one thing at a time, so both can be handled in parallel.

crash.name: Service crashed
crash.symptom: The service process exited. The machine still answers ping, but its port is closed.

restart.note: The process is back; the logs show a one-off crash.

origin: A nightly job on {node} ran out of file handles and the service exited.
{node} hit an unhandled error after the morning traffic spike.
A config reload on {node} went wrong and the process died.
crash.effect: every call it makes to {origin} is refused

dns.name: DNS resolution failing
dns.symptom: Clients can't resolve hostnames. Connecting by IP address still works, but nobody remembers the numbers.

fixdns.note: Resolver configuration restored; names resolve again.

restart.note: The restart reloaded the cache, but the bad config returns as records expire.

origin: A typo slipped into {node}'s resolver config during a 'quick' change.
{node}'s upstream resolver was swapped for one that doesn't answer.
dns.effect: it can't look up {origin}'s names, so its requests fail
evidence: ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached
zone jungle/IN: loading from master file failed: bad dotted quad

dhcp.name: DHCP pool exhausted
dhcp.symptom: No addresses left in the pool. New devices get no lease and fall back to 169.254.x.x, which can't reach anything.

expandpool.note: The pool is widened from /26 to /24; new devices get leases.

restart.note: Restarting doesn't create addresses: the pool is still full.

origin: A batch of new sensors joined {node} and took every free address.
Someone shrank {node}'s DHCP range while tidying up.
dhcp.effect: new devices that reach it through {origin} get no address
evidence: dhcpd: no free leases on subnet 10.4.0.0/24

cable.name: Damaged cable
cable.symptom: 20% packet loss and CRC errors on one port. A crocodile chewed the patch cable.

replacecable.note: New cable fitted; the CRC errors are gone. It was the physical layer.

restart.note: Software restarts don't fix a damaged cable (layer 1).

origin: A crocodile chewed through {node}'s uplink cable.
A falling branch crushed the cable into {node}.
cable.effect: its traffic through {origin} keeps getting dropped
evidence: $ ip -s link show eth0   → CRC errors: 48,113
physical layer flapping: carrier lost 37× in 5 min

route.name: Missing route
route.symptom: The router lost its route to the southern islands; packets come back as ICMP 'destination unreachable'.

fixroute.note: The static route is restored; traffic flows again.

failover.note: The standby router works for now, but its routing table is stale.

origin: A route to {node} was deleted during maintenance.
{node} learned a bad route from a neighbour.
route.effect: packets it sends via {origin} never arrive
evidence: static route to 10.0.0.0/8 points at a dead next hop

ddos.name: DDoS flood
ddos.symptom: Requests ×40 from thousands of sources. A bison stampede is hammering one endpoint.

blockacl.note: Firewall ACL drops the attacking sources; real users get through.

ratelimit.note: Rate limiting buys time but also turns away some real users. The attack continues.

restart.note: Restarting doesn't stop traffic that is still arriving.

origin: A botnet of a million bison found {node} on the open internet.
Someone posted {node}'s address on a stampede forum.
ddos.effect: the flood through {origin} is crushing it too
evidence: top talkers: 41,000 sources, none seen before today

worm.name: Worm infection
worm.symptom: An unknown process copies itself over every connection it can reach.

warning.text: A worm signature is circulating and this node is unpatched.

patch.note: Patched and cleaned; the hole it used is closed.

quarantine.note: Isolated on its own VLAN: it can't spread, but it's still infected.

restart.note: The worm survives reboots: it's in the startup scripts.

origin: Someone on {node} opened a banana-themed email attachment.
An unpatched service on {node} was found by a scanning worm.
evidence: CVE match: unpatched SMB service, exploit in the wild

cert.name: Expired TLS certificate
cert.symptom: Clients reject the TLS handshake: the certificate's validity date has passed.

warning.text: The TLS certificate expires soon. Renew it now and nobody notices.

disabletls.note: Refused: turning off TLS would send passwords in clear text. Renew the certificate instead.

origin: {node}'s certificate auto-renewal has been failing quietly for weeks.
{node}'s certificate was issued by hand a year ago, and nobody set a reminder.
evidence: clients: x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid

leak.name: Memory leak
leak.symptom: RAM use grows 2 GB a minute and the system is swapping. Something never frees its memory.

patch.note: The code that never freed memory is fixed.

restart.note: Memory is freed for now; the leak will fill RAM again.

failover.note: The standby takes over with clean memory; the same bug leaks there too.

origin: The new release on {node} forgets to free its cache.
A slow memory leak in {node} has been growing since Monday.
evidence: RSS grows linearly since the last deploy: nothing is freed

disk.name: Disk full
disk.symptom: Disk at 100%. Writes fail and logs can't rotate.

warning.text: Disk at 85% and climbing: old snapshots are piling up.

cleanup.note: Old snapshots removed; writes work again.

origin: {node}'s snapshots haven't been pruned since spring.
A debug log on {node} was left on, writing gigabytes an hour.
evidence: writes failing: No space left on device (ENOSPC)

heat.name: Thermal throttling
heat.symptom: CPU at 98 °C and throttling its clock speed: the vents are clogged with leaves.

clearvents.note: Vents cleared; the temperature is back to 55 °C.

restart.note: It cooled while rebooting; it will heat up again.

origin: The afternoon sun is on {node}'s rack and a fan is clogged with leaves.
{node}'s cooling vent is blocked by a fallen palm frond.
heat.effect: {origin} answers so slowly that it times out
evidence: CPU throttled to 800 MHz to survive

power.name: Power supply failed
power.symptom: Lightning hit the rack and the primary power supply is dead. The redundant one is idle.

failover.note: Switched to the redundant power supply.

restart.note: Nothing to restart: there's no power.

origin: A storm cloud's lightning struck {node}'s power supply.
evidence: System Power : off   Last Power Event : ac-failed

deploy.name: Bad deploy
deploy.symptom: v2.4 went out and the error rate is 30%. There was no schema change: v2.3 is still compatible.

warning.text: A deploy of v2.4 is scheduled. Canary it first: a bad build then reaches only a few users.

rollback.note: Back on v2.3, which is compatible: the errors stop.

fallforward.note: No hotfix is ready yet. v2.3 is compatible, so rolling back is faster and safe.

restart.note: Restarting runs the same broken v2.4.

origin: v2.4 went out to {node} without a canary.
A Friday-afternoon deploy reached {node}.
deploy.effect: one in three requests to {origin} returns an error
evidence: REVISION 41 (10 min ago)  ← errors began here
error rate 0.1% → 38% right after the deploy

migration.name: Bad deploy with migration
migration.symptom: v2.4 migrated the database schema and the error rate is 30%. v2.3 can't read the new tables.

fallforward.note: Hotfix v2.4.1 shipped; it works with the new schema.

rollback.note: v2.3 can't read the migrated schema: rolling back would break it further.

origin: v2.4 went out to {node} with a database migration.
migration.effect: one in three requests to {origin} returns an error
evidence: schema half-applied: column `bananas_v2` exists, code still reads `bananas`

disparity.name: Replica disparity
disparity.symptom: The replicas' checksums disagree: two copies report two different banana counts.

resync.note: Replicas re-copied from the primary; the checksums match.

origin: A replica of {node} fell behind during a network blip and nobody noticed.
Writes to {node} went to the wrong replica during a failover.
disparity.effect: it reads stale or conflicting data from {origin}

loop.name: Routing loop
loop.symptom: Packets circle between two routers until their IP TTL (a hop count) reaches 0 and they're dropped.

fixroute.note: The route that pointed back is fixed; packets reach their destination.

restart.note: Routes were relearned, but the bad static route returns.

origin: Two routers near {node} each think the other has the best path.
A static route on {node} points back at itself.
loop.effect: packets through {origin} go round in circles
evidence: $ tcpdump -c 5 -e   → the same frame 5× in 2 ms
switch CPU 100%, MAC table flapping between ports 3 and 7
no spanning tree: two cables close a loop

broadcast.name: Broadcast storm
broadcast.symptom: A looped cable floods the switch with broadcasts; Spanning Tree was turned off on this switch.

enablestp.note: STP blocked the redundant port; the storm stops.

replacecable.note: The cables are fine; it's the loop they form.

origin: Someone plugged both ends of a cable into {node}.
A redundant link was added to {node} without Spanning Tree.
broadcast.effect: the broadcast flood from {origin} swamps it
evidence: ARP who-has storms from one misconfigured host
every host on the segment spends its CPU reading them

vlan.name: VLAN misconfiguration
vlan.symptom: Ports were put on the wrong VLAN: the tree frogs can't reach their default gateway.

fixvlan.note: Ports are back on VLAN 20; the gateway answers.

restart.note: The port configuration survives a restart.

origin: A port change on {node} put servers in the wrong VLAN.
{node} was re-cabled and the VLAN tags weren't updated.
evidence: $ show interfaces trunk   → VLAN 40 not allowed on Gi0/1
hosts in VLAN 40 can't reach their gateway
a trunk change this morning dropped the tag

upstream.name: Upstream failure
upstream.symptom: Nothing is wrong here: it's suffering from a problem next door.

bgp.name: BGP route hijack
bgp.symptom: Half the internet now thinks our addresses live somewhere else. Traffic is walking off to a stranger's network.

rpki.note: Invalid route announcements are rejected: only we may announce our prefix.

morespecific.note: Longer prefixes win, so most traffic comes home. The bad route is still out there.

fixroute.note: Our own routes are fine: the bad one is announced by someone else.

origin: A neighbouring network fat-fingered a route and claimed {node}'s addresses.
A mischievous magpie network announced {node}'s prefix to the whole internet.
bgp.effect: its traffic through {origin} wanders off to a stranger's network
evidence: traceroute leaves the jungle after 3 hops

ransomware.name: Ransomware
ransomware.symptom: Files are being renamed to *.locked and a note demands 400 bananas.

warning.text: A machine is quietly beaconing to an unknown server every 60 seconds.

restore.note: Clean files are back from backups the attacker could not touch.

quarantine.note: Isolated: the encryption can't reach more shares. The locked files are still locked.

restart.note: The files stay encrypted after a reboot.

origin: Someone on {node} opened 'free_bananas.pdf.exe'.
An old remote-desktop port on {node} had a guessable password.
ransomware.effect: its shared files on {origin} are locked
evidence: backups: immutable copy from 02:00 is intact

creds.name: Credential stuffing
creds.symptom: Millions of logins with passwords leaked from other sites. A few are working.

mfa.note: A stolen password alone no longer gets anyone in.

ratelimit.note: Fewer guesses per second, but they keep coming.

blockacl.note: The guesses come from everywhere: there's no short list of sources to block.

origin: A password dump from another site turned up, and {node} is the obvious place to try it.
A bot-herder rented a million home routers to try passwords on {node}.
creds.effect: accounts used through {origin} are being taken over
evidence: $ grep 'login failed' auth.log | wc -l   → 3,881,027 in 10 min

ntp.name: Clock drift
ntp.symptom: This machine thinks it is seven minutes in the future. Logins and certificates are being rejected as 'not yet valid'.

ntp.note: Clock back in step: tokens and certificates make sense again.

rotatecert.note: A new certificate looks 'not yet valid' to a clock that's wrong too.

origin: {node}'s time server was quietly switched off last week.
A virtual machine on {node} was paused and resumed, and its clock never caught up.
ntp.effect: tokens signed on {origin} look like they come from the future
evidence: $ chronyc tracking   → System time: 412.7 s slow of NTP time
JWT error: token used before issued (iat in the future)

mtu.name: MTU black hole
mtu.symptom: Small requests work; big downloads hang forever. Ping is fine, which makes it extra confusing.

mss.note: TCP segments now fit the tunnel; nothing needs fragmenting.

restart.note: The packets are still too big for the path.

origin: A new VPN tunnel on {node} shrank the path, and a firewall eats the 'packet too big' messages.
{node} got jumbo frames turned on, but the river link didn't.
evidence: $ ping -M do -s 1472 core   → Frag needed and DF set (mtu = 1400)
ICMP type 3 code 4 blocked by a firewall rule

splitbrain.name: Split brain
splitbrain.symptom: Two copies both think they are in charge and both accept writes. Their data is drifting apart by the second.

fence.note: One primary again: the stale one is powered off and will rejoin as a replica.

readonly.note: No new conflicts, but nobody can write anything either.

failover.note: Failing over makes a third leader. Not helpful.

origin: A network hiccup cut {node}'s cluster in half and each half elected a leader.
Someone restarted {node}'s cluster manager with quorum checks switched off.
splitbrain.effect: reads through {origin} get different answers each time
evidence: writes accepted on both sides since 14:02

exfil.name: Data exfiltration
exfil.symptom: Someone is smuggling data out, one tiny DNS question at a time.

warning.text: Odd TXT lookups for random-looking subdomains, all night.

sinkhole.note: The smuggler's domain now leads nowhere, and every stolen key is useless.

blockacl.note: This exit is blocked; they'll look for another.

restart.note: The implant starts again with the machine.

origin: A poisoned browser plugin on {node} has been whispering secrets for a week.
A quiet intruder set up camp in {node} and is packing up the silverware.
exfil.effect: secrets that pass through {origin} are being copied out

stampede.name: Cache stampede
stampede.symptom: A popular cache entry expired and ten thousand requests all ran to the database at once.

warmcache.note: Hot keys are warm again and only one request refills each miss.

ratelimit.note: The herd is held back at the gate. The cache is still cold.

restart.note: A restarted cache is an empty cache: even more misses.

origin: Every key on {node} was set to expire at exactly midnight.
A flash sale on golden bananas emptied {node}'s cache.
stampede.effect: requests through {origin} wait in a very long queue
evidence: all keys share one TTL: they expired together

zeroday.name: Zero-day exploit
zeroday.symptom: A brand-new bug with no patch yet. Strange requests are making the service do things it shouldn't.

virtualpatch.note: The firewall now blocks the exploit pattern until a real patch ships.

quarantine.note: Cut off from the rest; it's still vulnerable.

patch.note: There is no patch yet: that's what zero-day means.

origin: A clever weasel found a bug in {node} that nobody knew about.
A proof-of-concept for {node}'s web framework was posted an hour ago.
zeroday.effect: requests from {origin} carry the exploit along
evidence: vendor advisory: CVE-2026-1337, no fix available
process spawned /bin/sh from the web server

supplychain.name: Poisoned dependency
supplychain.symptom: Last night's build picked up a library update with a hidden backdoor.

pinrevert.note: Rebuilt from a signed, pinned lockfile: the bad version is gone.

rollback.note: Yesterday's build runs for now; the next build will pull the bad version again.

origin: A maintainer's account for banana-utils was taken over and a new version shipped.
{node}'s build used a package with a name one letter off from the real one.

fixroute.label: Correct the routing table
fixroute.cmd: ip route replace default via 10.0.0.1 dev eth0

ratelimit.label: Rate-limit traffic
ratelimit.cmd: tc qdisc add dev eth0 root tbf rate 200mbit burst 32k

blockacl.label: Block attackers with an ACL
blockacl.cmd: iptables -A INPUT -m set --match-set stampede src -j DROP

disabletls.label: Disable TLS
out: refused by policy: TLS can't be disabled in production
(credentials would cross the jungle in clear text)

fixvlan.label: Move ports to the right VLAN

morespecific.label: Announce more-specific /24s
out: longest prefix wins: most traffic comes home

mfa.label: Force MFA + reset sessions
mfa.cmd: idp policy set mfa=required && idp sessions revoke --all
out: MFA now required for every account
stolen passwords alone no longer work

ntp.label: Resync the clock (NTP)
out: System time: 0.000014 s fast of NTP time

mss.label: Clamp TCP MSS to the path MTU
mss.cmd: iptables -t mangle -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu

fence.label: Fence the stale primary (STONITH)
out: writes go to one place again

readonly.label: Switch to read-only mode
out: no new conflicts can be written

sinkhole.label: Sinkhole the C2 domain + rotate keys
sinkhole.cmd: rpz add evil-banana.example CNAME . && vault rotate --all

warmcache.label: Warm the cache, coalesce requests
out: request coalescing on: one miss, one DB query

virtualpatch.label: Deploy a WAF virtual patch
out: exploit attempts now blocked at the edge

pinrevert.label: Pin deps + rebuild from lockfile
pinrevert.cmd: git checkout lockfile@verified && make build verify-sbom

timeloss.name: Time to Loss (game term)
timeloss.text: Lucky Monkey's own timer: seconds until the next consequence. Not IP TTL (a hop count) and not DNS TTL (how long a record may be cached).

process.name: Processes and ports
process.text: A service is a running process listening on a port. The machine can be up (it answers ping) while the service is dead.

dns.name: DNS
dns.text: The Domain Name System turns names into IP addresses. If it fails, connections by IP still work, but names don't.

dhcp.name: DHCP
dhcp.text: DHCP hands out IP addresses from a pool, as time-limited leases. With an empty pool, new devices get no address.

physical.name: Physical layer
physical.text: Layer 1: cables, ports and signals. CRC errors and packet loss on one port often mean a bad cable, which no software fixes.

routing.name: Routing
routing.text: Routers forward packets using a routing table. Without a route, the packet is dropped and ICMP reports 'destination unreachable'.

ddos.name: DDoS
ddos.text: A distributed denial of service floods a target from many sources. Rate limits buy time; filtering the sources (ACLs) stops it.

patching.name: Patching and segmentation
patching.text: Worms exploit unpatched holes and spread across the network. Isolating a node (a separate VLAN) stops the spread; patching removes the hole.

tls.name: TLS certificates
tls.text: TLS encrypts connections and proves identity with a certificate that expires. Renew it before it does; never just turn encryption off.

memory.name: Memory and swap
memory.text: A leak keeps claiming RAM until the system swaps to disk and crawls. A restart frees it for a while; only a code fix stops it.

storage.name: Storage capacity
storage.text: A full disk makes every write fail. Rebooting doesn't free space: delete or move data, or add capacity.

thermal.name: Thermal throttling
thermal.text: Hot CPUs slow themselves down to survive. Cooling (airflow, clean vents) is the fix.

redundancy.name: Redundancy and failover
redundancy.text: A spare component (a second power supply, a standby server) takes over when the primary fails, if one was there to begin with.

rollback.name: Rollback
rollback.text: Undo a bad change by going back to the previous version, as long as that version still works with today's data.

migration.name: Schema migrations
migration.text: A deploy that changes the database schema can't simply be rolled back: the old version can't read the new tables. Fix forward.

replication.name: Replication
replication.text: Replicas are copies of a database. When they disagree, re-copy them from the authoritative primary.

ipttl.name: IP TTL
ipttl.text: Each IP packet carries a TTL hop count; every router subtracts 1, and at 0 the packet is dropped. That stops a routing loop from circling forever.

stp.name: Spanning Tree
stp.text: STP finds loops between switches and blocks a redundant port, so broadcasts can't circle and multiply into a storm.

vlan.name: VLANs
vlan.text: VLANs split one switch into separate networks. A port on the wrong VLAN can't reach its own subnet's default gateway.

origin.name: Root cause and blast radius
origin.text: One fault at its origin spreads effects to everything that depends on it. Fixing the symptoms downstream does nothing; fix the origin and the symptoms clear by themselves.

bgp.name: BGP and RPKI
bgp.text: Networks announce which addresses they own with BGP. Anyone can announce anything, so RPKI signs who may announce what, and routers reject the rest.

ransomware.name: Ransomware and immutable backups
ransomware.text: Ransomware encrypts files and asks for payment. Backups that cannot be changed (immutable, offline) are what make it a bad day instead of a disaster.

auth.name: Credential stuffing and MFA
auth.text: Leaked passwords from one site get tried on others. Multi-factor authentication means a password alone isn't enough.

time.name: Clock sync (NTP)
time.text: Certificates, tokens and logs all depend on the time. NTP keeps clocks in step; a few minutes of drift breaks logins.

mtu.name: MTU and MSS
mtu.text: Every link has a largest packet size (MTU). If 'packet too big' messages are blocked, big transfers silently hang. Clamping TCP MSS avoids it.

quorum.name: Split brain and quorum
quorum.text: A cluster needs a majority (quorum) to pick one leader. Without it both halves may lead; fencing (STONITH) powers off the stale one.

exfil.name: Exfiltration and DNS tunnels
exfil.text: Attackers hide stolen data in ordinary-looking traffic, even DNS lookups. Sinkholing their domain and rotating keys cuts them off.

cache.name: Cache stampede
cache.text: When a hot cache entry expires, many requests miss at once and hammer the database. Request coalescing and staggered expiry prevent it.

zeroday.name: Zero-days and virtual patches
zeroday.text: A zero-day has no vendor patch yet. A WAF rule that blocks the exploit pattern (a virtual patch) protects you until one ships.

supplychain.name: Supply-chain attacks
supplychain.text: Your code is only as safe as what it depends on. Pinned, signed versions and an SBOM let you rebuild from known-good parts.

notices.text: Cache hit ratio 94% at {node}: most requests never touch the database.
{node}: CPU 61 °C, a little warm but within limits.
Unusual traffic to {node}: just the tree frogs' weekly sync.
{node}: cached DNS records expired after their TTL (300 s) and were refreshed.
Bandwidth between the islands at 40%: plenty of headroom.

roles.monkey: The Guardian: a core hub. Many paths run through it.
roles.router: A router forwards packets between networks using its routing table. If it fails, everything that reaches the rest of the network through it is cut off.
roles.river: A network segment where devices join, get addresses (DHCP) and talk to each other.
roles.banana-cache: A cache keeps copies of frequently used data close by, so requests don't have to go all the way to the database.
roles.temple: An application server: runs services that other nodes call.
roles.server: A general-purpose server running services. Can crash, leak memory or overheat.
roles.firewall: A firewall allows or blocks traffic by rules (ACLs). The first line against attacks.
roles.database: A database stores records, often as several replicas that must agree.
roles.volcano: A high-performance compute node: fast, hot, and sensitive to cooling.
roles.ai-core: A compute node running heavy workloads.
roles.vault: Backup storage. Backups only count if they can be restored.
roles.switch: A switch connects devices on the same network and forwards frames by MAC address. Loops between switches cause broadcast storms unless Spanning Tree blocks them.
roles.terminal: A client machine: a user's view of the network.
roles.lizard: A monitoring probe watching a segment.
roles.lake: A data lake: large, cheap storage for raw data and analytics.
roles.dns: A DNS server turns names into IP addresses. Without it, names stop working even though the network is fine.
roles.balancer: A load balancer spreads requests across several servers so none is overloaded.
roles.queue: A message queue holds messages in order until consumers are ready, smoothing out bursts.
roles.monitor: Monitoring: collects metrics and warns before things break. If it's unreachable you lose your warnings.
roles.auth: Authentication: checks identities and holds TLS certificates others trust.
roles.cdn: A content delivery network caches content close to users.

difficulties.name: Recruit
difficulties.blurb: Coached training shift. A gentle, scripted start.

difficulties.name: Operator
difficulties.blurb: A normal day on call. Trouble shows up one or two at a time.

difficulties.name: Veteran
difficulties.blurb: Faster timers and coordinated attack campaigns.

difficulties.name: Jungle Legend
difficulties.blurb: Everything at once. The bison have brought friends.

campaigns.name: The Great Stampede
campaigns.text: A herd of botnet bison is charging the front door while someone tries every password on the login page.

campaigns.name: The Velvet Python
campaigns.text: A sneaky crew is slipping in quietly. Watch for data leaving by odd doors.

campaigns.name: Nightfall
campaigns.text: The big one, right before closing time: routes, files and floods all at once.
